children: Bitcoin sank to its lowest level since September 2024 on Friday, November 20. The main spark, according to Reuters, came from outside crypto: a growing worry that investors have paid too much for artificial intelligence stocks.
That anxiety rattled markets and weighed on risk assets broadly.
Bitcoin dropped as much as 6% during the session. Intraday lows were reported between $55,533 and $57,716.
For context, that is a long way from where the asset sat a little over a year ago. Bitcoin peaked above $126,000 in October 2025 and has since lost more than 50% of its value.

The selling didn't stay politely in the spot market. Roughly $2 billion to $2.4 billion in long crypto futures positions were liquidated over a 24-hour window, and Bitcoin futures made up more than $1 billion of that total.
Institutional money was heading for the exits too. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $582 million on November 19, the day before Bitcoin reached its two-year low.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq dropped more than 4% on November 20. When the tech-heavy index and Bitcoin take a hit on the same day for the same reason, it gets hard to argue the two live in separate worlds.

Friday's slide erased the gains Bitcoin built in the environment that followed the US election. AI valuations were the headline worry, but they weren't the only weight on the market. Concerns about the profitability of heavy AI infrastructure spending added to the gloom, along with rising borrowing costs that have dented investor confidence.

Crypto also had problems of its own making. The fallout from a Binance hack in late October still hung over the market, and Democratic gains in the midterms brought fresh regulatory uncertainty for an industry that had been counting on a friendlier policy backdrop.

Friday told a different story on Bitcoin's identity. Bitcoin traded like a high-beta tech stock, falling alongside the Nasdaq on worries that had nothing to do with blockchains, halvings or hash rates.

The ETF data deserves close attention. Spot Bitcoin ETFs were supposed to bring steady, patient institutional capital into the market. A $582 million outflow in a single day shows those same vehicles can carry money out just as efficiently as they brought it in.
Liquidations of $2 billion or more clear out a lot of overextended positions. Leverage is the other piece to watch, as thinner participation tends to mean sharper moves in both directions.

Rising borrowing costs make speculative assets less attractive compared to safer options that pay a yield, and that pressure doesn't care whether the speculative asset is an unprofitable AI startup or a cryptocurrency.

On the policy side, the midterm results add a layer of uncertainty. The industry had been operating with expectations of a more supportive Washington, and any shift in that outlook could affect everything from exchange operations to how institutions approach the sector.
The Binance hack in late October meant crypto entered this risk-off stretch already on the back foot. Bitcoin is now more than 50% below its October 2025 peak.

title: Bitcoin falls to two-year low as AI valuation fears spill into crypto
